Yet even then, fighting for those same democratic values in much harder circumstances, we had two enormous advantages over today's generation. First, we had absolutely no doubt that the future would be free and better. Second, we had absolutely no doubt that we would be part of that change. Today's young people are losing both of those certainties, and that's decisive for democracy. So we need to start by bringing back hope and belief in the future, and the sense of empowerment, before they are replaced by resignation, by fear, then anger, then hate — which is what's happening. The second ingredient — I'll go faster now — is facts, and a reasonable amount of reason. Maria Ressa, the journalist from the Philippines who won the Nobel Peace Prize a couple of years ago, said that in a society with no agreement on facts there can be no democracy. That's a fact, and it describes the situation in most of our countries rather accurately. There's no more agreement — not just disagreement on the facts themselves, but on whether we should even agree on facts at all. Everyone is now free to select their own set of facts and choose a reality that suits their emotional, ideological, or other needs. Once you're there, democracy can't function. Much of this is emotionally driven — for reasons that are sometimes justified, sometimes not, sometimes a result of perception, sometimes reality — but it's there, and so far our best response has been a very rational one. We need to find better ways of dealing with this emotionally driven rejection of facts, reason, knowledge, and science, without adding to the tension. We've gotten as far as telling people: listen, democracy is great, your problem is that you are media illiterate, and you got your facts wrong. That's not going to convince anyone that democracy is great. The third ingredient is confidence — trust in democracy. This connects to the first. People have lost trust in democracy, often for good reasons, because they're disappointed and frustrated — not in democracy or democratic values themselves, but in the way democracy has been administered to them by politicians. More and more of them feel left out, marginalized, they have the feeling their legitimate expectations and interests are being ignored. There's too much hypocrisy, too many double standards, from people whose mouths are full of democratic values. That has consequences. Restoring that confidence and trust won't be easy. The fourth ingredient: integrity, competence, and effectiveness. It's an unfair fight — democracies are up against authoritarian populists, who are rage farmers. The worse things are, the better it is for them, at least for a while. What democracy has to offer is effective solutions to people's problems. That's tough, difficult, unfair — but it has to be done if we want to preserve democracy and make it more resilient. Finally, common decency: not just speaking about it, but practicing and showing the most fundamental, universal human values — solidarity, respect for human dignity, empathy — all in very short supply today. Instead, we live in a world where many political leaders act in a completely transactional way, where the only way to win is for someone else to lose, where the only way to win is to inflict pain on someone else. Democracy cannot work under those conditions — and we're talking about politicians who consider themselves democrats. So there's a lot on the plate. What is the Council of Europe doing about it? I invite you to look at our website — I won't go through it all, but we have, I think, genuinely impressive policy work addressing each of the areas I've mentioned. We have a relatively new Secretary General, from Switzerland, who launched the New Democratic Pact for Europe as an exercise in the critical thinking I mentioned earlier — about what we do, how we do it, how we can do better, how we bring others into building a more resilient democracy. What we cannot do from the Council of Europe — what cannot be done from Strasbourg, or Brussels, or even Geneva — is bring democracy somewhere, or save it, without the participation of citizens. We can't do it. Democracy isn't built top-down, it has to be built bottom-up. When you have that alliance — citizens, civil society, local authorities, media — I think we can still succeed. We must. I'll stop here, because my watch is telling me it doesn't look too good. I will just add that personally, I remain an optimist about the future of democracy. A very, very worried optimist, but an optimist still. And if you're looking for inspiration: the last time I was in Ukraine, sitting in a cellar during an air raid, I had a conversation with a young Ukrainian woman. She said: we can't afford pessimism here in Ukraine. Think of the alternatives. Thank you.
